hook: A city caps rents and the waiting list for apartments triples. A state sets a minimum price for milk and the dairies pour out what no one buys. A tax of \$1 a can on kombucha raises the shelf price by 80 cents, not \$1. Each of these is a policy that changes price signals, and each one can be traced on the supply and demand graph.

figure.caption: A \$2 tax on ferry rides: buyers pay \$6, sellers keep \$4, revenue is \$80 and deadweight loss \$10. Invented data for practice.

chain.cause: A per-unit tax is collected from sellers
chain.effect: supply shifts up (left) by the amount of the tax
buyers pay a higher price, sellers keep a lower one, and fewer units are traded
the surplus on the units no longer traded is lost: a deadweight loss

chain.cause: The units still traded are taxed
chain.effect: the government collects the tax times the new quantity, paid partly by each side

ideas: Price ceiling (maximum) binds below equilibrium: a shortage, and only Qs is traded. Price floor (minimum) binds above equilibrium: a surplus, and only Qd is traded.
A per-unit tax shifts supply up by the tax: buyers pay more, sellers keep less, quantity falls. Revenue = tax × the new quantity.
A per-unit subsidy shifts supply down: buyers pay less, sellers get more, quantity rises. Cost = subsidy × the new quantity, the whole rectangle.
Deadweight loss: total surplus lost on units not traded (or traded past the equilibrium), the triangle between demand and supply.
Tax incidence: the less elastic side of the market bears more of the tax, whoever hands it to the government. A quota cuts quantity and raises the price.

misconception.wrong: The cost of a subsidy is the small area between the curves past the old quantity, and tax revenue runs out to the original quantity.
misconception.right: Both rectangles use the quantity after the policy. The subsidy cost is the per-unit subsidy times the new, larger quantity: the whole rectangle between the two prices. Tax revenue is the tax times the new, smaller quantity. The triangle between the curves is deadweight loss.

summary: Price ceilings, price floors, quotas, taxes and subsidies change the price signals and the quantity traded. A binding ceiling (below equilibrium) causes a shortage; a binding floor (above it) a surplus; in both, fewer units are traded. A per-unit tax shifts supply up, raises the price buyers pay, lowers the price sellers keep and raises revenue equal to the tax times the new quantity; a subsidy does the reverse at a cost of the subsidy times the new quantity. In a market that was efficient, each of these creates a deadweight loss, and the burden of a tax falls more on the less elastic side.
